Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being reminded of the event by others
Being around people in authority or uniform

Threat.value: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

vignette:
Javier was twenty-two when he was abducted after his late shift as a janitor. Two men forced him into a dirty blue sedan, the same model he would later see in driveways across the suburb where he worked as a maid. For three days they held him in a concrete room, a television playing looped footage of other captives while they beat and burned him. They mocked his terror, forcing him to smile for a grainy camera. When they finally released him on a roadside, he walked home in a daze and never spoke of it.

In the years since, divorcing his wife and drifting through cleaning jobs, Javier has learned to scan every street for that blue sedan. The sight of one-even a different model, just similar-floods him with the smell of gasoline and stale smoke. News reports of cartel violence or abductions freeze him in front of a screen, his heart slamming against his ribs. What confuses him most is that any burst of happiness, a child laughing or a client thanking him warmly, now feels dangerous. It is as though his body remembers being forced to perform joy, and any genuine positive emotion is a trap that will lead back to that room.

He has become an expert at vanishing. When a friend starts to ask about his past, he finds an excuse to leave. Clients who wear uniforms-security guards, police officers, even a mail carrier-make him cross the street or cancel appointments. He has taken to smoking half a pack a day on his breaks, telling himself the nicotine steadies his hands. The smoke gives him a few minutes of numbness before the next trigger.

The threat never stops. He wakes multiple times a night to check the locks and listen for footsteps, certain that someone has found him. An unexpected touch from a coworker or a stranger brushing past him on the sidewalk sends him into a startle so violent he sometimes drops his cleaning supplies. Every unfamiliar face approaching him, especially men in groups, triggers a cold certainty that they are coming for him again. He has come to believe that strangers pose a constant danger, and his vigilance is the only thing keeping him alive. Living in that state of constant threat, ordinary sights - a car idling too long, a neighbor's unfamiliar voice - began to feel like signals he could not ignore, each one confirming that danger was closing in again.

These fears feed each other in a loop he cannot escape. A glimpse of a blue car makes his throat tighten and his palms sweat-the trigger directly ignites a sense of imminent threat. That threat, in turn, drives him to avoid the street altogether, to quit that job site, to light another cigarette. But avoidance only sharpens his attention: the more he dodges, the more he sees blue cars everywhere, the more he expects danger around every corner. When he sees an older man in a uniform, he immediately reads hostility into the man's posture, and the resulting spike in threat convinces him that his caution was justified. Smoking has become its own trigger, because the act of lighting a cigarette in public draws attention, and any approaching stranger while he smokes is interpreted as a threat. Each strategy he uses to feel safe makes the world feel more dangerous, and every new danger reinforces his need to hide.

Javier finally sought help because his avoidance cost him his only steady account: a client complained he had left without finishing the living room. He had seen a news clip about a kidnapping on their television and had to leave immediately. Now he is down to two houses a week and can barely afford rent. He smokes so much that his chest aches. He is terrified that he will never stop feeling hunted, yet he is more afraid that if he lets his guard down, the men in the blue sedan will find him again.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that the sense of threat causes the patient to experience or perceive more triggers; rather, threat leads to maladaptive strategies which in turn increase triggers, but the direct causal relationship from threat to triggers is absent.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the sense of threat causes the patient to experience or perceive more triggers; rather, threat leads to maladaptive strategies which in turn increase triggers, but the direct causal relationship from threat to triggers is absent.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
